installation.note: ps is a built-in command available on all Linux systems by default

overview.summary: ps displays information about currently running processes. Unlike htop or top, ps provides a snapshot of processes at the time it's executed rather than continuously updating. It's useful for scripts and one-time process queries.
when_to_use: View running processes at a specific point in time
Find process IDs (PIDs) for specific programs
Check process status and resource usage
Use in scripts for process monitoring

syntax.description: ps can be used with various options to display different information about processes. Without options, it shows processes in the current terminal session.

misconceptions.title: ps shows real-time process information
misconceptions.misconception: ps continuously updates like top or htop
misconceptions.reality: ps takes a snapshot of processes at the moment it runs. It doesn't continuously update. For real-time monitoring, use top or htop instead.
misconceptions.tip: Use ps for one-time queries or scripts. Use top/htop for continuous monitoring.

misconceptions.title: ps -aux is the same as ps aux
misconceptions.reality: The correct syntax is 'ps aux' (without the dash before aux). ps -aux would try to find a user named 'x', which may cause errors.
misconceptions.tip: Always use 'ps aux' without a dash before 'aux'

misconceptions.title: ps shows all processes by default
misconceptions.misconception: ps displays all processes in the system
misconceptions.reality: ps without options only shows processes from your current terminal session. Use 'ps aux' or 'ps -ef' to see all processes.
misconceptions.tip: Use ps -e, ps aux, or ps -ef to see all processes on the system

common_pitfalls.issue: Forgetting that ps is a snapshot
common_pitfalls.description: Expecting ps to show continuously updated information
common_pitfalls.solution: Remember that ps shows processes at a single point in time. Run it multiple times or use watch ps aux for periodic updates, or use top/htop for continuous monitoring.

common_pitfalls.issue: Using ps -aux instead of ps aux
common_pitfalls.description: Adding a dash before aux causes incorrect behavior
common_pitfalls.solution: Always use 'ps aux' without the dash. The 'aux' are options that should not have a leading dash.
Learn common STAT values: R (running), S (sleeping), D (uninterruptible sleep), Z (zombie), T (stopped). Use 'man ps' for complete list.

best_practices: Use 'ps aux' for comprehensive process listing with resource usage
Combine ps with grep to find specific processes: ps aux | grep processname
Use custom format (-o) to show only columns you need: ps -o pid,cmd,%cpu
Sort output by resource usage: ps aux --sort=-%cpu | head -10
Use 'ps auxf' or 'ps -ef' to see all processes, not just current terminal
Filter out grep from results: ps aux | grep processname | grep -v grep
Use pstree or ps auxf to understand process relationships
Save output for analysis: ps aux > processes.txt
performance_tips: ps is very fast as it only takes a snapshot, not continuous monitoring
Limit output with head/tail if you only need top/bottom processes: ps aux | head -20
Use custom format (-o) with fewer columns for faster output
Combine with grep for filtering rather than parsing all output
For scripts, use -o with specific columns to reduce parsing overhead

additional_notes.process_states: Common STAT values: R (running), S (interruptible sleep), D (uninterruptible sleep), T (stopped), Z (zombie), X (dead)
additional_notes.formatting: ps supports different output formats: BSD-style (ps aux), Unix-style (ps -ef), and custom (-o flag)
additional_notes.scripting: ps is ideal for scripts because it's non-interactive and takes a snapshot rather than running continuously
additional_notes.comparison: Use ps for quick checks and scripts. Use top/htop for interactive monitoring. Use pgrep/pkill for finding/killing by name.
